subject: Intel's worst day since 1974, and your next laptop
bodyMarkdown:
Intel had its worst day on the stock market since 1974 on Friday, and the cause was the AI boom working too well. Memory chips have become so expensive that PC makers are cutting their build plans, and that cost is heading for the price of your next laptop.

## What Intel actually said

Intel reported third quarter results on Thursday and guided fourth quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, against analyst expectations closer to $17.1 billion. Adjusted earnings guidance of 25 cents a share landed well under the 44 cents the street wanted. The number that did the real damage sits in client computing, the division that sells chips for ordinary PCs. It brought in $8.1 billion in the third quarter, and Intel told investors to expect a decline of more than 20 per cent in the fourth. In its filing, Intel pointed to higher component prices, particularly memory, along with constrained IT budgets and customers managing inventory more tightly, and said it expects those conditions to worsen in the fourth quarter and persist into 2027. The stock closed down almost 29 per cent. Yahoo Finance reported Friday that it was Intel's worst single day since July 5, 1974.

## Why memory got so expensive

The mechanism is simple enough to be annoying. Samsung, SK hynix and Micron make nearly all of the world's DRAM, and all three have shifted their best capacity toward **high-bandwidth memory** (the stacked, costly kind that AI accelerators need to keep their compute fed). Ordinary PC memory comes off the same lines, so every wafer that goes to an AI data centre is a wafer that does not become a laptop module. TrendForce expects conventional DRAM **contract prices**, the negotiated prices that manufacturers pay rather than what you see at retail, to rise another 10 to 15 per cent this quarter. Android Headlines reported last month that Samsung expects supply to stay tight into 2028, with its 2027 HBM4 output already sold out. Intel's own forecast has industry PC shipments falling about 12 per cent this year and another 10 per cent in 2027.

## The bill the hyperscalers are running

October was the month investors started asking out loud who pays for all of this. CNBC reported that the Nasdaq fell 5.3 per cent on the month, its steepest drop since March 2025, and the S&P 500 fell 1.82 per cent on Friday alone to 7,580. Alphabet shed roughly $758 billion in market value over October, its worst month since going public in 2004, after reporting negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion when analysts had pencilled in negative $2.70 billion. Amazon spent $77.3 billion on capital expenditure in one quarter against a FactSet consensus of $58.7 billion. Microsoft went the other way, trimming its capital spending forecast to $170 billion from $175 billion, and its shares held up fine. I do not think the market has turned against AI. I think it has started charging a premium for companies that can fund the buildout from operations instead of from debt and share sales.

## The takeaway

If you are planning to buy a laptop, phone or desktop in the next year, buy earlier rather than later, and pay for more memory than you think you need, because Gartner's February forecast had 2026 PC prices running 17 per cent above 2025 and smartphones 13 per cent higher. Watch the fourth quarter DRAM contract settlements in December, because they decide whether this is a one-year squeeze or a problem that runs to 2028. For anything you hold in tech, ask whether the company pays for its AI spending out of cash flow or out of borrowing and equity, since October treated those two very differently. I am also watching whether this shows up on the goods side of Canadian CPI, since we import all of this hardware.
